ai-at-work.title: Microsoft president says UK is best placed to drive AI regulation
ai-at-work.excerpt: Microsoft president Brad Smith calls for urgent AI regulation, saying milk and washing machines have more oversight than AI companies.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Microsoft's president Brad Smith is lobbying the UK to lead global AI regulation, arguing that current oversight of AI companies is laughably weak compared to everyday products. This matters because digital workplace leaders will eventually inherit whatever regulatory framework gets built, and unclear rules create real compliance headaches down the line. That said, hearing a Microsoft exec demand regulation from anyone is rich coming from a company that's spent decades lobbying against every privacy and antitrust rule they could dodge, so forgive me if I wait to see the actual commitments before I believe the conversion.

ai-at-work.title: This AI startup says it can generate permit-ready blueprints in minutes
ai-at-work.excerpt: Blueprints AI, a bootstrapped startup based in Santa Monica, developed software that produces code-compliant construction blueprints from a photo, PDF, or sketch.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: An AI startup claims it can turn photos or sketches into fully permit-ready construction blueprints in minutes, supposedly eliminating weeks of manual drafting work. This matters because if it actually works, architects and construction firms could redirect skilled labor toward higher-value design thinking instead of grinding through compliance documentation. That said, I've seen plenty of "just take a photo" automation promises crater the moment they hit real-world messiness, so I'm holding the applause until someone shows me a permit officer actually stamping one of these things without notes.

digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece about how new AI models and features frequently break existing workflows and processes, despite vendor promises about stability. This matters because digital workplace leaders are increasingly betting their productivity infrastructure on AI integrations, and silent failures or degraded performance can tank employee adoption faster than you can say "technical debt." The real kicker is that we're essentially paying vendors to experiment on our production systems while they figure out consistency, which feels like outsourcing our IT department's QA testing to the general public.

digital-culture.title: Fear of being ‘too much’ silences women leaders. Here’s how to ask anyway
digital-culture.excerpt: “I don’t know if I came across super harsh or not. At some point, I lost sense of how I was showing up.” That was my client after having a hard conversation with one of her leaders about getting the r
digital-culture.dwp_take: A leadership coach is highlighting how women leaders second-guess themselves after advocating for basic resources, worried they'll be perceived as demanding or difficult. This matters to digital workplace pros because psychological safety and equitable access to tools directly impact productivity, retention, and whether your best talent actually stays. The irony is that the same assertiveness celebrated in male leaders gets rebranded as "harsh" when women do it, which is less a communication problem and more a culture problem that spreadsheets won't fix.

digital-culture.title: Take your full maternity leave
digital-culture.excerpt: If Rati Sahi Levesque could rewrite one rule of corporate America, it would be this: Make your own schedule. There’s nothing wrong with working at your own pace—as long as you get the work done. The M
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company is featuring a piece about flexible work arrangements where a female leader advocates for employees to control their own schedules rather than being locked into rigid 9-to-5 structures. This matters to digital workplace pros because flexible scheduling directly impacts talent retention, particularly for parents, and it forces companies to rethink how they measure productivity beyond seat time. The irony, of course, is that we've been saying "results only matter" for years now, yet most organizations still treat presence like it's a personality trait.

digital-culture.title: You can be a great mother and love your work
digital-culture.excerpt: OnlyFans CEO Keily Blair says women (and mothers in particular) often feel they need to apologize for wanting to work, succeed, and take joy in their careers. Her message: You don’t have to wear ambit
digital-culture.dwp_take: Keily Blair, CEO of OnlyFans, is pushing back against the guilt culture that tells women they need to choose between motherhood and career ambition, arguing they can do both without apology. This matters because digital workplaces are still packed with unspoken rules that make mothers feel like they're failing on both fronts if they dare admit they actually like their jobs. The real insight here isn't revolutionary, but it's refreshing to hear someone say it plainly instead of wrapping it in wellness language about "having it all."
